lessonTitle: Development of the Heart: Heart Tube, Looping, Septation and the Fetal Circulation

blocks.text: A newborn looks pink and well on day 1, but by day 2 becomes progressively blue, and the only thing keeping a few babies alive is a small fetal vessel that normally closes within hours or days. To see why, you need to know how the heart is built from a simple tube in the fourth week, and how the fetal circulation is rewired at birth.

blocks.markdown: **Formation of the heart tube.** The heart is the first functioning organ. In week 3 mesoderm in the **cardiogenic area**, cranial to the neural plate, forms two **endocardial tubes**. Lateral folding of the embryo brings the tubes together and they fuse in the midline at about day 22 into a single **primitive heart tube**. The tube has an inner endothelial lining (**endocardium**), a gelatinous layer (**cardiac jelly**) and an outer **myocardium**; epicardium is added later from cells that migrate over the surface. The tube starts to beat around day 22-23 and blood circulates by the end of week 3 to 4. From tail to head the tube has five dilatations: the **sinus venosus** (receives venous blood), **primitive atrium**, **primitive ventricle**, **bulbus cordis** and **truncus arteriosus**.

blocks.title: Cardiac looping
blocks.text: Cardiac looping is the bending of the elongating heart tube during days 23-28. The tube bends to the right (a D-loop), bringing the primitive atrium and sinus venosus to a position dorsal and cranial to the ventricle and bulbus cordis, and giving the heart its basic adult arrangement. Failure of rightward looping, or looping to the left, can lead to dextrocardia.

rows: Smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum), coronary sinus, oblique vein of the left atrium; contributes to the venae cavae
Trabeculated parts of the right and left atria (auricles)
Trabeculated part of the left ventricle
Trabeculated part of the right ventricle and the smooth outflow tracts (conus cordis) of both ventricles
Ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk (via the aorticopulmonary septum)
blocks.caption: Derivatives of the primitive heart tube.

blocks.markdown: **Septation of the atria (weeks 4-6).** Endocardial cushions form in the atrioventricular canal and divide it into right and left channels. A crescent-shaped **septum primum** grows down from the roof of the common atrium toward the cushions, leaving a gap, the **ostium primum**. Before this closes, perforations in the upper part of the septum primum coalesce to form the **ostium secundum**. A second, thicker, crescent-shaped ridge, the **septum secundum**, grows down to the right of the septum primum, leaving an oval opening, the **foramen ovale**. The lower part of septum primum acts as a one-way **flap valve**: blood passes from the right atrium to the left atrium but cannot flow back. An atrial septal defect (ASD) arises from deficient septum primum or secundum; the **secundum ASD** at the fossa ovalis is the most common, and a **patent foramen ovale** persists in a sizeable minority of adults because the flap fails to fuse.

**Septation of the ventricles and outflow tract.** A **muscular interventricular septum** grows up from the floor of the ventricle; the gap above it, the interventricular foramen, is closed by the **membranous septum**, formed by growth of tissue from the endocardial cushions and the outflow cushions. A defect here gives a **ventricular septal defect (VSD)**, the commonest congenital heart anomaly, usually in the membranous part. In the outflow tract, **truncal and bulbar ridges** (populated by neural crest cells) grow and spiral toward each other and fuse into the **aorticopulmonary septum**, which divides the outflow into the aorta and the pulmonary trunk with a spiral twist. Abnormal septation causes **persistent truncus arteriosus** (no division), **transposition of the great arteries** (failure to spiral) and **tetralogy of Fallot** (anterior displacement of the septum, producing pulmonary stenosis, a VSD, an overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy).

blocks.title: Linking the septum to a defect
blocks.prompt: A child has a defect in the interventricular septum, pulmonary stenosis, an aorta overriding the defect and a thickened right ventricle. Identify the condition and the embryological explanation.

steps.text: The four features (VSD, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, right ventricular hypertrophy) define tetralogy of Fallot.

The primary cause is anterior displacement of the aorticopulmonary septum, which narrows the right ventricular outflow (pulmonary stenosis) and widens the aorta so that it overrides the septal defect, which is a malaligned VSD.
Right ventricular hypertrophy is secondary to the outflow obstruction. The right-to-left shunting that occurs across the VSD, if obstruction is marked, causes cyanosis.

blocks.answer: Tetralogy of Fallot, from anterior displacement of the aorticopulmonary septum.

blocks.markdown: **The fetal circulation.** The placenta, not the lungs, oxygenates fetal blood. Oxygenated blood (about 80% saturated) leaves the placenta in the **umbilical vein**. Most bypasses the liver through the **ductus venosus** to the inferior vena cava and right atrium. Because of the flap valve, much of the oxygen-rich IVC blood streams through the **foramen ovale** into the left atrium, then to the left ventricle and ascending aorta, supplying the coronary and cerebral circulations. Deoxygenated blood from the superior vena cava passes through the right atrium and right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk; because the collapsed lungs have a high **pulmonary vascular resistance**, most of this blood bypasses the lungs through the **ductus arteriosus** into the descending aorta. Blood returns to the placenta through the two **umbilical arteries** (branches of the internal iliac arteries).

rows: Ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of liver)
Shunts blood right atrium to left atrium
Shunts blood from pulmonary trunk to aorta
blocks.caption: Fetal shunts and their adult remnants.

blocks.markdown: **Changes at birth.** At the first breaths the lungs expand and fill with air, pulmonary vascular resistance falls sharply and pulmonary blood flow rises. Return of blood from the lungs raises left atrial pressure. When the umbilical cord is clamped, placental flow ceases and venous return to the right atrium falls. The left atrial pressure now exceeds the right and pushes the septum primum against the septum secundum, so the **foramen ovale closes functionally** (anatomical fusion takes months to years, and it stays probe-patent in a minority). The **ductus arteriosus** constricts in response to the rise in blood oxygen and a fall in prostaglandin levels, closing functionally in hours to a few days. Failure of closure gives a **patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)**, with a continuous 'machinery' murmur; prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors (as a pharmacology teaching example, indomethacin or ibuprofen) promote closure, while prostaglandin E1 can be used to keep the duct open in babies whose survival depends on it, such as some with transposition of the great arteries.

blocks.title: Shunt ratio in a left-to-right shunt
blocks.prompt: A child with a ventricular septal defect has pulmonary blood flow Qp of 7.5 L/min and systemic blood flow Qs of 5.0 L/min. Calculate the Qp:Qs ratio and explain its meaning.

steps.text: The shunt ratio is pulmonary flow divided by systemic flow.
A ratio above 1 means the lungs receive more flow than the body: there is a net left-to-right shunt, so some blood recirculates through the lungs. The extra 2.5 L/min is the net shunted volume.

blocks.answer: Qp:Qs = 1.5, indicating a net left-to-right shunt of 2.5 L/min.

blocks.title: Why the ductus arteriosus matters
blocks.text: In the fetus, high pulmonary resistance and low systemic resistance (the placenta is a low-resistance bed) direct blood through the ductus from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. After birth pulmonary resistance falls and systemic resistance rises, so a persisting duct shunts blood from the aorta to the pulmonary artery (left to right).

points: The heart tube forms from the fusion of paired endocardial tubes at about day 22, with five dilatations that loop to the right by day 28.

Atrial septation uses the septum primum and secundum with the foramen ovale as a flap valve; ventricular septation uses the muscular and membranous septa; the aorticopulmonary septum divides the outflow tract.

In the fetal circulation the ductus venosus, foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the liver and lungs; at birth falling pulmonary resistance and rising left atrial pressure close the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus constricts.

questions.stem: The primitive heart tube is formed by fusion of paired endocardial tubes. Which process brings these tubes together?

options.text: Lateral folding of the embryo
Cranial folding that places the septum transversum caudal to the heart
Neural crest migration
Regression of the notochord

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lateral folding brings the two tubes to the midline where they fuse.
distractorRationale.b: Cranial folding repositions the heart ventrally but does not fuse the paired tubes.
distractorRationale.c: Neural crest contributes to the outflow septum but does not fuse the tubes.
distractorRationale.d: The notochord does not play this role.

questions.explanation: Lateral folding of the embryo in week 4 brings the paired endocardial heart tubes together in the midline where they fuse into a single tube at about day 22. Cranial folding moves the heart tube into the thorax.

questions.stem: Which part of the primitive heart tube gives rise mainly to the trabeculated part of the left ventricle?

options.text: Primitive ventricle
Bulbus cordis
Sinus venosus
Truncus arteriosus

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the primitive ventricle forms the trabeculated left ventricle.
distractorRationale.b: The bulbus cordis forms the trabeculated right ventricle and outflow tracts.
distractorRationale.c: The sinus venosus forms the smooth part of the right atrium and coronary sinus.
distractorRationale.d: The truncus arteriosus forms the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

questions.explanation: Looping places the primitive ventricle to the left of the bulbus cordis; the primitive ventricle becomes the left ventricle, and the proximal bulbus cordis becomes the right ventricle.

questions.stem: In the fetus, which pathway delivers the best-oxygenated blood to the coronary and cerebral circulations?

options.text: Umbilical vein, ductus venosus, IVC, right atrium, foramen ovale, left atrium, left ventricle, ascending aorta
Umbilical artery, ductus arteriosus, descending aorta
Superior vena cava, right ventricle, pulmonary trunk, ductus arteriosus
Pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle

questions.correctOptionText: Umbilical vein, ductus venosus, IVC, right atrium, foramen ovale, left atrium, left ventricle, ascending aorta

distractorRationale.a: Correct: oxygenated blood from the placenta is directed across the foramen ovale to the left side.
distractorRationale.b: Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the placenta.
distractorRationale.c: This describes the route of deoxygenated SVC blood towards the descending aorta.
distractorRationale.d: Fetal pulmonary venous return is small because the lungs are collapsed.

questions.explanation: The umbilical vein carries the most oxygenated blood; via the ductus venosus and IVC it reaches the right atrium, where the position of the foramen ovale and its flap valve direct much of it across the foramen ovale to the left heart and ascending aorta.

questions.stem: Which change is the principal reason the foramen ovale closes after birth?

options.text: Left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure, pressing the septum primum against the septum secundum
Right atrial pressure rises above left atrial pressure
Umbilical vein flow increases
The ductus venosus dilates

questions.correctOptionText: Left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure, pressing the septum primum against the septum secundum

distractorRationale.a: Correct: increased pulmonary venous return and reduced right atrial pressure reverse the gradient.
distractorRationale.b: The pressure gradient reverses in the opposite direction.
distractorRationale.c: The umbilical vein is occluded at birth.
distractorRationale.d: The ductus venosus also closes after birth.

questions.explanation: Lung expansion lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and increases pulmonary venous return to the left atrium, while clamping the cord removes the placental return to the right atrium. The reversed pressure gradient pushes the septum primum flap against the septum secundum, closing the foramen ovale.

questions.stem: A premature infant has a continuous machinery murmur at the left infraclavicular area, bounding pulses and signs of heart failure. Which vascular connection persists?

options.text: Between the pulmonary trunk (left pulmonary artery) and the descending aorta
Between the left and right atria
Between the umbilical vein and inferior vena cava
Between the left and right ventricles

questions.correctOptionText: Between the pulmonary trunk (left pulmonary artery) and the descending aorta

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is a patent ductus arteriosus.
distractorRationale.b: This describes an atrial septal defect or patent foramen ovale.
distractorRationale.c: This describes the ductus venosus, which closes after birth.
distractorRationale.d: This describes a ventricular septal defect, which causes a pansystolic murmur.

questions.explanation: A continuous machinery murmur reflects blood flowing from the higher-pressure aorta to the pulmonary artery throughout the cardiac cycle through a patent ductus arteriosus, which is more common in premature infants.

questions.stem: A patient with an atrial septal defect has a pulmonary blood flow Qp of 9.0 L/min and a systemic blood flow Qs of 4.0 L/min. Calculate the Qp:Qs ratio.
questions.explanation: The shunt ratio equals pulmonary flow divided by systemic flow: 9.0 / 4.0 = 2.25. A ratio above 1 indicates a net left-to-right shunt (here through the atrial defect), where the right heart handles substantially more flow than the left would for the systemic circulation alone.

questions.stem: True or false: In the fetus, most of the blood ejected by the right ventricle passes through the lungs.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Because pulmonary vascular resistance is high in the fetus, most right ventricular output passes through the ductus arteriosus into the aorta. Only a small proportion goes through the lungs.

questions.stem: Describe how the primitive heart tube forms and loops, and state the adult derivatives of the sinus venosus, primitive atrium, primitive ventricle and bulbus cordis.
markingGuide: Paired endocardial tubes from cardiogenic mesoderm fuse at about day 22 by lateral folding to a single heart tube with endocardium, cardiac jelly and myocardium.
Five dilatations: sinus venosus, primitive atrium, primitive ventricle, bulbus cordis, truncus arteriosus.
Looping to the right (D-loop) at days 23-28 brings the atrium cranial and dorsal.

Sinus venosus: smooth right atrium and coronary sinus; primitive atrium: trabeculated parts of atria; primitive ventricle: trabeculated left ventricle; bulbus cordis: trabeculated right ventricle and outflow tracts.
questions.explanation: Fusion produces the tube, which then loops; each segment has a specific adult derivative.

questions.stem: Outline how the atria and ventricles are septated, and explain how deficiencies in these processes produce atrial and ventricular septal defects.
markingGuide: Atrial: septum primum grows from the roof toward endocardial cushions; ostium primum closes; perforations form ostium secundum.
Septum secundum grows to the right of septum primum, leaving the foramen ovale with the flap valve of septum primum.
Ventricular: muscular interventricular septum grows upward from the floor; membranous septum closes the interventricular foramen using endocardial cushions and outflow cushions.
ASD: deficient septum primum or secundum (secundum ASD commonest); patent foramen ovale if the flap fails to fuse.
VSD: failure of the membranous septum to form, the commonest congenital heart defect.
questions.explanation: Each septum comes from separate growing tissues that meet and fuse; failure of any step leaves a communication.

questions.stem: Describe the changes in the circulation at birth. Include the fate of the foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus, ductus venosus and umbilical vessels, and the consequence of a persisting ductus arteriosus.
markingGuide: Lungs expand, pulmonary vascular resistance falls and pulmonary blood flow and left atrial pressure rise.
Cord clamping removes the low-resistance placental circuit and reduces right atrial pressure; left atrial pressure exceeds right, closing the foramen ovale (later fossa ovalis).
Ductus arteriosus constricts due to increased oxygen and decreased prostaglandins, becoming the ligamentum arteriosum.
Ductus venosus becomes ligamentum venosum; umbilical vein becomes ligamentum teres hepatis; umbilical arteries become medial umbilical ligaments.
Persisting ductus: patent ductus arteriosus with continuous machinery murmur and left-to-right shunt.
questions.explanation: Pressure changes at birth close the fetal shunts. A persisting duct creates an aorta-to-pulmonary-artery shunt.
